title: Curt Cignetti for President
author: Tim Daly
summary: Tim Daly uses the turnaround of Indiana football under coach Curt Cignetti, who answered a question about recruiting with "I win. Google me," as a model for American literacy policy. After a new round of tepid international reading results, he says responses split between panic and dismissal, while states lack goals or plans. He argues the picture is better than the headlines: the US ranks 10th of 83 countries in reading, with a very high ceiling and an unusually low floor, so raising the floor is the key. He recalls past American leaps in high school completion, research, manufacturing and cars as evidence that the country wins once it commits. His proposal is for governors to set state reading goals that add up to topping PISA within 15 years, backed by named leaders, funding and annual public accounting, early literacy investment, patience with the science of reading, a focus on teen reading, and relentless attention to boring execution.
points: The US ranks 10th in reading on PISA but has the world's widest gap between top and bottom students, so the main task is raising the floor.
Most states have no clear or public learning goals, which makes accountability impossible and leaves policy to panic or shrugging.
Daly proposes a governors-led 15-year goal to top PISA, with a responsible official, funding and an honest annual accounting.
Progress from literacy reforms takes years, so leaders must hold their nerve and invest in the boring work of consistent classroom execution.
quotes: How, a snide reporter asked, could you possibly sell this program to recruits? His response: “It’s pretty simple. I win. Google me.
While we have boatloads of panic and dismissal, we never seem to have a goal or a plan. I mean that literally.
The Center on Reinventing Public Education recently found 11 states with no statewide learning goals whatsoever. Only 13 had data-driven, time-bound goals that had been communicated publicly.
But beneath our solid overall performance, we have a gigantic problem. The gap between our top students (90th percentile) and our lowest-scoring students (10th percentile) is the largest in the world
Good readers are less likely to live in poverty or be victims of crimes. Becoming number one would be transformational for countless families and communities.

Each governor should appoint someone to be responsible for the plan, put money behind it, and publish an honest accounting of where things stand each year. Fifteen years spans several administrations - which is the point.
It takes years to improve instruction before test scores move assertively in the right direction. During that period, decision-makers must hold their nerve.

That’s how reading instruction works. It’s a fistful of small moves repeated consistently by teachers who know what to look for and how to address challenges. And those teachers set a high bar for their students.
